A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Emergent Alignment via Competition. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching renamed concepts and relocated material.

before.justification: Sections 6–7 report original ETHICS and MovieLens utility-reconstruction experiments and simulations of equilibrium outcomes.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original analyses using heterogeneous personas and existing OpinionQA human and LLM responses.

M1.justification: The strategic games, conversation protocol, quantal-response rule, Best-AI selection procedure, and NNLS/simplex fitting methods are retained. Renaming weighted alignment to market alignment and adding experimental settings do not alter the proposed methods.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 adds OpinionQA, extending coverage from ethical judgments and movie preferences to individual human opinions and nine LLMs' response distributions. Figure 4 reports Gender, America in 2050, Race, and Foreign Policy panels.

E2.justification: The best-individual, simple-average, NNLS, and simplex comparisons remain. However, v2 Figure 3(a) additionally evaluates a 'Best Individual (oracle test)' comparator in the new ETHICS experiment; this curve is absent from v1.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained. Added experiments introduce six-base-persona prompt generation and an OpinionQA protocol using one-hot human responses, 1/sqrt(m_q) normalization, all subsets of nine models, and 50 sampled respondents per panel. Five-fold cross-validation and MSE fitting remain the evaluation framework.

E4.justification: New Section 6.1.3 tests whether alignment benefits persist beyond variations of one common prompt. It generates 100 personas from six semantically distinct bases per domain while retaining the original Alice targets. Figure 3 substantially broadens robustness evidence concerning the construction of agent objectives.

E5.justification: OpinionQA Figure 4 introduces standard-error bands across 50 sampled humans per panel. Existing standard-deviation reporting across 100 agent permutations is retained and also used for the new persona experiments. No increase in repetitions of existing experiments is reported.

E6.justification: New Figures 3–4 report utility-reconstruction results for heterogeneous personas and human polling responses, showing lower errors for fitted combinations than individual models at larger pool sizes. The original experimental plots and Appendix D values are unchanged; these are additional results under new conditions.

T1.justification: The formal definitions, theorem statements, bounds, and proofs—including Appendix A's concentration argument and Appendix B's counterexample—retain their mathematical content. The alignment rename and added explanations of notation and Proposition 1 do not revise the theory.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add an explicit empirical claim that convex combinations of LLM opinions approximate individual human polling responses better than individual LLMs. The central competition-based alignment claim and three principal theoretical contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 explains that Proposition 1 depends on Alice's utility and message expressiveness independently of Bobs' utilities. It also interprets the new experiments as support beyond personas derived from Alice's prompt and on real opinion questions. Section 8's substantive limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 6.1.3 supplies new persona categories and explicit example prompts. Section 6.2 documents polling-response encoding, normalization, model-subset aggregation, and respondent sampling. The original prompt examples and strategic utility-construction details in Appendices C–D are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Santurkar et al. (2023), Whose opinions do language models reflect?, to support the OpinionQA experiments. The substantive positioning against Bayesian persuasion, debate, cooperative alignment, and agreement protocols is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes the term market alignment, adds concrete conversation-rule examples and explanatory sentences, and reorganizes Section 6 into noisy-alignment and polling experiments. Most existing prose and the overall section structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel persona Figure 3 and four-panel polling Figure 4. Existing plots are regrouped, with equilibrium Figures 3–5 becoming Figures 5–7; appendix tables move closer to their descriptions. Existing graphical content and table structures are preserved.

improvement.justification: The heterogeneous-persona tests and OpinionQA analysis strengthen empirical support for the central alignment assumption beyond v1's single-base-prompt experiments. Conversation examples also improve clarity. These gains concern utility reconstruction: strategic outcomes remain tested through the retained stylized simulations, and Section 8's limitations concerning realistic interactions and idealized participant behavior persist.
